title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling & runbooks (comprehensive playbook)
author: Ava Ramirez
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime reference material: architecture, kernel scheduling strategy, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, release notes, known issues, operational runbooks, and the runtime team wiki pointers. Intended audience: runtime engineers, SREs, performance engineers, and product owners working on inference scalability and reliability.

Goals
- Provide a single, searchable reference for runtime design decisions and operational procedures.
- Give repeatable profiling and benchmarking recipes for reproducible performance investigations.
- Codify kernel scheduling rules and heuristics used in production.
- Offer runbooks for common incidents and upgrade operations.

1) Runtime architecture (summary)

Short intro: The serving runtime is a GPU-optimized inference engine with an orchestration layer that performs model routing, batching, KV-cache management, and quantization-aware execution. The runtime supports hosted, dedicated, and private deployments with the same control-plane APIs.

High-level components:
- Frontend API gateway: authentication, rate limiting, request normalization, initial filtering.
- Router: policy-based routing (latency, cost, region, model-version).
- Batch-manager: continuous batching service that groups requests by model and sequence-length distribution.
- Executor (worker): GPU process that runs model kernels and KV cache; supports CPU-only fallback.
- Cache layer: hot-prefix cache and KV-cache service (sharded per-instance).
- Observability pipeline: token-level tracing, latency histograms, token cost accounting, and per-model dashboards.

Cross-cutting design constraints:
- SLOs: p50 <= 80ms, p95 <= 250ms for small chat workloads (<=512 tokens) on standard configs; throughput targets are documented per instance type in the benchmark appendix.
- Deterministic fallbacks: if a model variant is unavailable, router selects a compatible quantized variant within the same semantic family.
- Isolation: tenant-resources are logically separated on Dedicated and physically separated in Private.

2) Kernel scheduling: principles and heuristics

Purpose: maximize GPU utilization while meeting latency SLOs by choosing execution kernels and when to preempt/slot requests.

Scheduling primitives:
- KernelSelection(model, batch_size, sequence_length, quantization_profile, device): picks the best kernel implementation and memory layout.
- SlotReservation(window_ms): short windows used by continuous batching to decide when to dispatch a batch.
- PreemptionPolicy: rules for interrupting long-running requests to service higher-priority traffic.

Key heuristics:
- Prefer fusion kernels for large-batch, long-seq workloads; prefer incremental kernels (streaming-friendly) for low-latency small requests.
- Use sequence-length bucketing: requests are assigned to buckets {<=64, 65-256, 257-1024, >1024}; batch formation happens only within a bucket.
- Quantization-aware choice: for int8 profiles, use kernels that favor lower precision accumulators to reduce memory pressure; fallback to float16 when numeric stability is at risk.
- Priority lanes: traffic labeled as "low-latency" (customer SLO) gets fast-lane preemption with a 10ms dispatch window; background jobs (batch embedding) use relaxed windows (up to 200ms).

Kernel selection table (examples)
| Model family | Sequence bucket | Preferred kernel | Notes |
|--------------|-----------------|------------------|-------|
| transformer-xl | <=64 | fused-attn-v2 | best p50 for short chat |
| llama-2 | 65-256 | kv-opt-stream | balanced latency/throughput |
| sliding-window | >256 | chunked-mem-opt | reduces peak memory |

Configuration knobs (defaults)
- slot_window_ms: 12
- max_batch_size_per_gpu: 64
- bucket_thresholds: "64,256,1024"
- preemption_enabled: true
- preemption_priority_cutoff: 0.9

3) Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

When to profile: regressions in p50/p95, memory spikes, unexplained OOMs, or before rolling a new kernel set.

Prerequisites:
- Access to staging cluster that mirrors production (same GPU family and driver).
- Profiling tools: nvprof/nsight, perf, custom in-house tracer (runtime-probe), and the benchmark harness (see Benchmarking suite).

Procedure:
1. Identify the workload and reproduce with a controlled traffic generator. Use the benchmark harness with the same prompt and sequence-length distribution.
2. Capture observability traces for a 10-30 minute window around the event: token latencies, scheduling decisions, kernel selections.
3. Run a micro-profile: single-request, single-GPU run with nvprof / Nsight to collect kernel timelines and memory snapshots.
4. Run a scaled profile: multi-worker run with runtime-probe to capture contention, PCIe/PCIe-switch traffic, and batch-formation patterns.
5. Compare kernel timelines against previous baseline artifacts (stored in s3://redwood-runtime-benchmarks/baselines/).
6. If a kernel regression is found, record: failing-commit, kernel-name, inputs, and reproduce command. Open a ticket with the runtime-kernel tag and attach artifacts.

Common commands
- Start micro-profile (example):
```
# Run single worker with nvprof
export RUNTIME_PROFILE=1
./runtime_worker --model llama-2-7b --device 0 --max-seq 512 --profile nvprof --out profile-output.nvvp
```
- Collect runtime traces (runtime-probe):
```
./benchmark_harness --workload chat --model llama-2-7b --concurrency 32 --duration 600 --emit-trace s3://redwood-runtime-benchmarks/traces/run-$(date +%s).json
```

Artifacts to capture
- nvprof/nsight captures (.nvvp), runtime-probe JSON traces, host-level metrics (iostat, nvidia-smi topo --matrix), kernel selection logs, and a reproducible driver/torch/onnx/cudnn manifest.

4) Benchmarking suite (overview + recipes)

Purpose: provide reproducible, automated benchmarks for throughput, latency SLOs, and unit cost estimates across instance types and model variants. Results are stored centrally and used for model onboarding, release gating, and capacity planning.

Bench harness components:
- workload definitions: chat-short, chat-medium, longform, embeddings-bulk, re-ranking.
- load generator: multi-host orchestrated tool that can replay recorded traffic or synthesize sequences.
- result store: S3 bucket + metadata store (benchmark DB) recording system config, driver versions, and artifacts.

Representative benchmark run (latency profile)
1. Prepare environment: pin drivers and CUDA versions from matrix in appendix.
2. Choose dataset: use "chat-short" prompts (see /datasets/chat-short/README).
3. Run:
```
./benchmark_harness --workload chat-short --model llama-2-7b-int8 --instances 4 --duration 900 --capture-metrics
```
4. Upload and register:
```
./benchmark_uploader --bucket redwood-runtime-benchmarks --run-metadata meta.json --artifacts ./results/
```

Benchmark metrics captured
- per-token latency histograms (p50,p90,p95,p99), GPU utilization, memory high-water mark, average batch size, and cost-per-1k-tokens estimate.

Benchmark pass criteria for release gating (example)
- p95(latency, chat-short) must be <= 1.5x baseline for same instance class.
- memory high-water mark must be <= 90% of GPU memory on the target instance.
- average batch size should not degrade more than 10% vs baseline unless explicitly allowed.

5) Release notes (runtime releases)

Format: each release entry includes release-version, date, highlights, performance impact, migration notes, and owner. Store release artifacts and benchmark diff.

Sample recent entries:
- v2026.12.03 (2026-12-03)
  - Highlights: Introduced fused-attn-v2 kernel for short-sequence chat models.
  - Performance impact: p50 improved by 18% for chat-short on A100-80GB; p95 unchanged.
  - Migration notes: no config changes required; enable via kernel_profile: fused-attn-v2 in model manifest to opt-in.
  - Owner: Marcus Lee

- v2027.01.10 (2027-01-10)
  - Highlights: Rolling out adaptive-slot-window scheduler; default slot_window_ms reduced from 20 -> 12.
  - Performance impact: improved p50 12% on mixed workloads; slight increase in p95 for >1024 token requests.
  - Migration notes: Users with longform workloads should consider pinning slot_window_ms to 20 in their deployment profile.
  - Owner: Priya Natarajan

Release checklist (pre-rollout)
1. Benchmarks: run gating suite and verify pass criteria.
2. Smoke tests: run end-to-end API smoke with canary traffic.
3. Observability: ensure dashboards populated and comparison baselines uploaded.
4. Rollout plan: canary -> region -> global, with automated rollback thresholds configured.

6) Known issues (operational)

This section lists recurring issues and temporary mitigations. Update with incident links and postmortems.

Issue: OOMs during long-sequence mixed workloads
- Symptoms: worker crashes with CUDA OOM; sudden memory high-water marks.
- Root causes: suboptimal kernel selection for mixed sequences causing large temporary buffers; buggy memory accounting in int8 path in driver vX.Y.Z.
- Mitigation:
  1. Force fallback kernel (chunked-mem-opt) by setting kernel_profile override in model manifest.
  2. Restart worker with --memory-overcommit=0.85 to constrain allocations.
  3. Patch: apply hotfix v2026.11.29-driver-patch and redeploy.

Issue: increased p95 after quantization changes
- Symptoms: p95 regression on chat-medium with quantized int8 models.
- Root causes: additional de-quantize steps introduced in pipeline; batching window interplay.
- Mitigation:
  - Re-evaluate quantization profile and enable mixed-precision kernels.
  - Temporarily revert to previous quantization profile and open ticket for kernel engineering.

7) Runbooks (operational playbooks)

Runbook: High p95 latency in production
1. Triage (0-5 mins): check dashboards (per-model p50/p95), check recent deploys (gitops), and check autoscaler events.
2. Containment (5-15 mins): enable fast-lane by setting route.priority for impacted customers; reduce max_batch_size_per_gpu to prioritize latency.
3. Diagnosis (15-60 mins): run profiling playbook (micro-profile and scaled-profile); review kernel selection logs for abnormal choices.
4. Remediation (1-3 hours): if a regression introduced in last deploy, roll back to previous runtime version. If caused by traffic shape change, tune slot_window_ms and bucket_thresholds.
5. Post-incident: file postmortem, update playbook, and schedule a retro with kernel owners.

Runbook: Worker OOM and restarts
1. Check node metrics and last worker logs for OOM stacktrace.
2. If OOM on init, inspect model manifest for memory settings and quantization flags.
3. If OOM during request handling, drain node and restart worker with smaller max_batch_size_per_gpu.
4. If persistent, cordon node and schedule replacement; open high-priority ticket for kernel team.

8) Team wiki & knowledge base pointers

Canonical pages (quick links):
- Serving runtime ops reference: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/serving-runtime-ops-reference-2026-03-04

- Kernel engineering playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-engineering-handbook

Onboarding checklist for new runtime engineers
- Read architecture overview and runbooks.
- Run the benchmark harness end-to-end for chat-short and embeddings-bulk.
- Shadow a production oncall for 2 weeks and perform at least one incident rotation.
- Complete runtime kernel training and pass the profiling quiz.

Appendix

Driver / software matrix (example)
| Component | Supported versions (recommended) | Notes |
|----------|----------------------------------|-------|
| CUDA | 11.8, 12.1 | Pin for consistency in benchmarks |
| cuDNN | 8.4+ | Use vendor-recommended builds |
| PyTorch | 2.1.x | runtime compiled against this set |
| NCCL | 2.14+ | required for multi-GPU collectives |
